title: Come to our house — inviting, accepting, declining
title_target: दिवाली पर हमारे घर आइए — divaalii par hamaare ghar aaiye
goal: Accept invitations, decline without offending, and calmly state your food limits — in a country where turning down an offer directly is almost never done.
bekal: stating what you don't eat or drink

dialogs.title: संवाद — A Diwali invitation
dialogs.intro: Priya invites Ani to her home. Look at line six: Ani turns down the offer "no need to bring anything", and that refusal is exactly what's expected — most polite conversation in India works this way.

lines.speaker: प्रिया:
lines.id: Ani, come to our house for Diwali.
lines.literal: Ani — ji, Diwali — on — our — house — come.

lines.speaker: प्रिया:
lines.id: The whole family will be there. Food, sweets, lamps.
lines.literal: whole — family — will-come. food, sweets, lamps.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: How can I do that? I'll bring something.

lines.speaker: प्रिया:
lines.id: All right, bring some sweets. But you don't have to.
lines.literal: good — is, sweets — take — come. but — necessary — not.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: And… one thing. I don't drink alcohol.
lines.literal: and… one — thing. I — liquor — not — drink(fem.).

lines.speaker: प्रिया:
lines.id: No problem! There isn't any in our house anyway.
lines.literal: some — thing — not! our — house — in — also — not — is(fem.).

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: And the food — I don't eat pork.
lines.literal: and — food — I — pig — of — meat — not — eat(fem.).

lines.speaker: प्रिया:
lines.id: Oh, we're vegetarian! Everything will be fine.
lines.literal: oh, we — after-all — vegetarian — are! all — fine — will-stay.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: Then it's settled. See you at Diwali!
lines.literal: then — settled. Diwali — on — meeting — is!

notes: **मैं क्या लाऊँ? — a new form, meaning "shall I …?".** It's the future without the -गा tail: **-ऊँ** (I), **-ए** (he/she), **-एँ** (we/you). *मैं क्या लाऊँ?* (what shall I bring?), *हम कब आएँ?* (when shall we come?), *क्या मैं बैठूँ?* (may I sit down?). ⚠️ This form is used for questions asking permission or advice, and it comes up constantly in polite conversation.

**"Don't bring anything" almost always means "bring something small".** An Indian host will turn down your offer once or twice out of politeness. The natural thing: bring **मिठाई** (sweets), fruit, or something typical from your country. ⚠️ Cut flowers are less common as a gift than in the West, and avoid sharp objects as presents — in some regions they're thought to bring division.

**Declining without saying "no".** The word **नहीं** exists, of course, but turning down an invitation or offer directly sounds harsh. What people say instead: **फिर कभी** (another time), **कोशिश करूँगी** (I'll try), **देखते हैं** (we'll see), **आज मुश्किल है** (today is difficult). ⚠️ This works both ways — if you hear one of these phrases, don't take it as "yes".

**Refusing second helpings takes its own technique, because your plate will keep getting filled.** What works: **बस बस, बहुत हो गया** while covering your plate with your palm, or **सच में, मैं भर गई हूँ** (honestly, I'm full). ⚠️ One refusal won't be taken seriously; you need to refuse two or three times, with a smile, and that's part of the conversation — not a sign that your host isn't listening.

**Stating your food limits actually makes things easier for your host.** Say it **before the day**, not at the table: *मैं शाकाहारी खाना खाती हूँ*, *मैं सूअर का माँस नहीं खाती*, *मैं शराब नहीं पीती*, *क्या यह हलाल है?*. ⚠️ And some real good news: **vegetarian households are very common in India**, so the issue often solves itself. Many families don't serve alcohol either.

**अतिथि देवो भवः — "the guest is a god".** This Sanskrit saying is truly alive in everyday Indian life, and the effect is real: guests get the best food, the best room, and attention that can feel overwhelming to foreigners. ⚠️ The best way to receive it isn't to refuse but to accept sincerely, praise the cooking, and invite them back later.

**पक्का — the word that seals a deal.** It means "sure, ripe, settled". *तो पक्का?* (so it's settled?), *पक्का!* (definitely!). Its opposite is **कच्चा** (raw, unripe, not settled). Both words have other uses too: a **पक्की सड़क** (paved road) versus a **कच्ची सड़क** (dirt road), and fruit that is **पक्का** (ripe).

aaj to mush-kil hai, phir ka-bhii

after: ⚠️ **सकना** = "can, may". It comes after the stem of another verb and agrees with the subject's gender: *मैं जा **सकती** हूँ* (I can go), *वह आ **सकता** है*, *आप बैठ **सकते** हैं*. You'll need this form very often, so learn the pattern: stem + सकना + होना.

grammars.title: Festivals and greetings

head: Festival
हिंदी
When
What to say
rows: होली मुबारक · बुरा न मानो, होली है!

after: ⚠️ **मुबारक** is the Arabic word *mubarak* you may know from "Eid Mubarak", and in India it's used for **all** festivals, not just Muslim ones: *दिवाली मुबारक* and *होली मुबारक* are said by everyone. It's one of the clearest examples of how the two layers of India's language have long shared with each other.

blocks.text: If you're invited to an Indian home, the following things are almost certain to happen — and knowing them in advance makes your first visit far more enjoyable.

items: **Shoes come off at the door.** Look for the pile of footwear outside; just follow suit.
**Tea or a drink arrives within five minutes**, before you've even settled in. Refusing it completely is a little rude; accept at least one.
**You'll be urged to eat more, again and again.** This isn't empty politeness — they mean it. See the note on refusing on the previous page.
**You'll be asked lots of personal questions** — age, salary, marital status, plans for children. It's a sign of acceptance, not nosiness. Answer as you like, or deflect with a smile.
**You may be asked to stay the night.** If you can't, give a clear reason and offer another visit: *आज नहीं, लेकिन अगली बार ज़रूर*.

⚠️ **Before you leave, thank whoever cooked** — usually the mother or grandmother, who often doesn't sit with you during the meal. *खाना बहुत स्वादिष्ट था, बहुत बहुत शुक्रिया* is a sentence that will be remembered for a long time.

blocks.title: Six sentences for visiting
items: **अंदर आ सकती हूँ?** — May I come in?
**आपका घर बहुत सुंदर है।** — Your home is beautiful.
**यह आपके लिए।** — This is for you. (while handing over your gift)
**खाना बहुत स्वादिष्ट है।** — The food is delicious.
**बस बस, बहुत हो गया।** — Enough, enough, that's plenty.
**अच्छा, अब मैं चलती हूँ। बहुत बहुत शुक्रिया।** — Well, I'll be going now. Thank you so much.

blocks.text: One sentence you'll often hear as you leave: **खाना खाकर जाइए** — "eat before you go". It's said even to a guest who dropped by for five minutes, even when it isn't mealtime, and it's meant sincerely. ⚠️ If you really must go, the answer that won't offend is **अगली बार ज़रूर, वादा** ("next time for sure, I promise") — and then really do come next time. In India an invitation is a relationship, not small talk, and keeping your word is noticed.
